incidents.title: Celebrity post spike
incidents.brief: A viral post triggers a sudden spike of 150,000 req/s, but the database is parsing and executing query plans for the exact same row over and over.
incidents.constraint: The content is identical across reads and does not change often.
incidents.question: Now what stops the viral post from pinning Postgres?

app: worker pool 512/512 busy, waiting on db
GET /post/8841 -> 200 in 1.7 s, no local cache header
db: SELECT * FROM posts WHERE id=8841 executed 149k/s
avg exec 0.1 ms, plan+parse dominates CPU

choices.label: Cache-aside Redis in front of Postgres for the hot post

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: In-memory caching cuts p95 from 1,800 ms to 120 ms and DB CPU from 92% to 16%. Tradeoff: when the hot key's TTL expires, every request misses at once (cache stampede).

choices.resultBody: The viral post is now served from Redis in about 1 ms per GET; only misses reach Postgres, so DB CPU falls from 92% to 16%. Cost: the key's TTL now decides freshness, and its expiry is a stampede waiting to happen.

choices.label: Postgres read replicas with read/write splitting

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Spreads SQL query load across read replicas, but replication lag causes stale reads and database replicas cost significantly more than caching.

choices.resultTitle: Read Replicas Absorb Read Volume (With Lag)
choices.resultBody: Reads for the post are spread across read replicas, dropping primary CPU to 28%. Cost: asynchronous replication means recent updates may be stale, and running database replica instances costs $850/mo.

choices.label: Raise the Postgres connection pool to 2,000 sockets

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Each Postgres connection is a process with its own memory; 2,000 of them contending for one hot row add lock and context-switch overhead, not throughput.

choices.resultBody: The hot row already sits in the buffer pool, so disk was never the limit. 2,000 backends now fight over the same row's buffer lock and CPU scheduler; context switching pushes p95 from 1,800 ms to 2,250 ms and errors triple.

hints: The same row is read 150,000 times while it barely changes.
The database is burning CPU re-answering an identical question, not waiting on disk.
Keep a copy of the answer somewhere much cheaper to read than Postgres.

mitigation.question: Postgres is at 92% and climbing. What buys you time right now?

choices.label: Flag off the live view counter and related-posts widget
choices.resultBody: Each view now runs 2 queries instead of 5, so DB CPU drops from 92% to 64% and p95 to 600 ms. The post itself still reads Postgres on every view, so the spike will return with the next share wave.

choices.label: Restart the Postgres primary to clear piled-up backends
choices.resultBody: Postgres was down for 40 seconds, then all 150,000 reads/s reconnected at once against an empty buffer cache. CPU hit 99% within a minute and errors spiked tenfold.

choices.label: Fail over reads to the standby in another availability zone
choices.resultBody: The failover cost 30 seconds of errors, and the standby now serves the identical hot row to the identical traffic from a colder cache. It reaches 94% CPU in two minutes.

incidents.title: ⚡ Second-Order Outage: Cache Stampede
incidents.brief: Two hours after deploying Redis, the 120-second TTL on the viral post key expired during peak evening traffic. 25,000 concurrent requests all missed simultaneously and dog-piled the primary database.
incidents.constraint: DB CPU spiked back to 96% and DB connection pool is locked under a thundering herd.
incidents.question: How do you mitigate the Cache Stampede (Thundering Herd)?

choices.label: Singleflight lock so one caller refills a missed key

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: One request per key regenerates it from Postgres while the other ~25,000 wait on the lock (or get the stale copy); waiters add a few ms of latency on each miss.

choices.resultBody: Singleflight lock prevented 25,000 duplicate queries. The cache was repopulated with a single DB read.

choices.label: Probabilistic early expiration (XFetch) on hot keys

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Asynchronous background workers refresh hot keys probabilistically before TTL expires.

choices.resultBody: Hot keys were refreshed shortly before expiry by whichever request drew the early-refresh lottery, so the key never went cold and DB CPU stayed near 20%.

choices.label: Set key TTL to 30 days so it never expires during traffic

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Static infinite TTL consumes Redis memory linearly and leaves stale content permanently.

choices.resultBody: Infinite TTL causes Redis RAM exhaustion when millions of keys accumulate, and edits to the post are never reflected.

hints: Multiple concurrent threads are attempting to recalculate the exact same expired key.
Consider synchronizing access so only one process queries the database on a cache miss (Singleflight/Mutex).
Or consider probabilistically refreshing the key in the background before TTL expires.

incidents.title: ⚡ Second-Order Anomaly: Replication Lag
incidents.brief: Users writing comments or updating their profiles immediately refresh the page, but see old data because asynchronous read replicas have a 650ms replication delay.
incidents.constraint: Users report critical data loss and duplicate submissions on recent updates.
incidents.question: How do you achieve Read-Your-Own-Writes consistency under asynchronous replication?

choices.label: Read from the primary for 5 s after a user's own write

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Guarantees read-your-own-writes for the author, while 99% of passive readers still query the replicas.

choices.resultBody: For 5 seconds after a write, the author's reads go to the primary, which covers the 650 ms lag with room to spare; the other ~99% of readers stay on replicas. Cost: a little extra primary load, and the window must be widened if lag ever grows past 5 s.

choices.label: Convert all read replicas to fully synchronous replication

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Every commit now waits for the slowest replica to confirm; one replica stall or network blip blocks all writes, trading availability for a guarantee only the author needed.

choices.resultTitle: Writes Now Wait on Every Replica
choices.resultBody: Stale reads stopped, but each comment commit now blocks until all replicas acknowledge it: p95 jumps from 180 ms to 465 ms, and when one replica paused for a disk snapshot every write in the system stalled with it.

choices.label: Make clients wait 1,000 ms behind a spinner before refetching

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: Arbitrary client sleeps do not guarantee replication catch-up and degrade user experience.

choices.resultBody: If replica lag exceeds 1,000ms under high load, the stale read bug returns. Client-side sleeps are not a distributed consistency mechanism.

hints: Asynchronous replication always has some lag. Only the author needs to see their write immediately.
Making every write wait for every replica fixes the author's view by slowing everyone else.
Consider routing only the writing user to the primary for a few seconds after a write (read-your-writes session token).

incidents.title: One Redis shard pegged during flash sale
incidents.brief: ShopNow's flash-sale SKU draws 180,000 reads/s. The Redis cluster is healthy except shard 7, which owns that key: 98% CPU, 420 ms p95, and timeouts spilling onto Postgres.
incidents.constraint: One key always hashes to one slot, so adding shards won't split it, and the sale ends in 40 minutes.
incidents.question: How do you take the single hot key off shard 7?

choices.label: In-process L1 cache on each app node, 1-second TTL
choices.resultTitle: Hot key absorbed in app memory
choices.resultBody: Each of the 60 app nodes now answers the SKU from local memory in well under a microsecond and asks Redis at most once per second, so shard 7 drops from 180,000 to ~60 reads/s. Cost: a price change can take up to 1 s to show on each node, and every node holds its own copy.

choices.label: Reshard the Redis cluster from 12 to 24 nodes
choices.resultBody: Resharding moved the SKU's slot to a fresh node, but all 180,000 reads/s for one key still land on whichever node owns it; slot migration traffic pushed p95 to 600 ms mid-sale.

choices.label: Raise the Redis client timeout from 50 to 500 ms
choices.resultBody: Calls that failed at 50 ms now wait and succeed, so errors fall from 310/s to 60/s and the spill onto Postgres stops. Shard 7 is still at 98% CPU, and busy app threads are climbing 3% a minute.

hints: Only one node in the cluster is hot; the others are nearly idle.
Hash slots decide placement, and a single key can never be split across shards.
The hottest reads could be answered before they ever leave the app process.

incidents.title: Profile cache hit rate stuck at 3%
incidents.brief: Trellis profile pages serve 60,000 req/s through Redis, yet the hit rate is 3%. Keys are built from the full URL, and every share link carries a unique ?ref= click ID. Postgres sits at 88% CPU.
incidents.constraint: Marketing needs the ?ref= parameter to keep reaching the analytics pipeline.
incidents.question: Why does the cache almost never hit, and what fixes it?

choices.label: Key on profile ID only, ignoring tracking params
choices.resultTitle: Every visit to a profile shares one key
choices.resultBody: The key becomes profile:{id}:v1, so the 400,000 daily share links for a popular profile all read one entry. Hit rate climbs from 3% to 96% and Postgres drops to 21% CPU. The ?ref= value is still logged by the app before the cache lookup, so analytics keep their click IDs.

choices.label: Raise the URL-keyed profile cache TTL to 24 hours
choices.resultTitle: Longer life for keys nobody reuses
choices.resultBody: Each click ID appears once, so a 24-hour TTL just keeps millions of single-use entries around. Redis memory grows by 30 GB and starts evicting, while the hit rate moves from 3% to 4%.

choices.label: Add two Postgres read replicas behind the profile app
choices.resultBody: Three databases now share the 58,000 misses per second, so each sits near 58% CPU and p95 halves. You pay about $2,400 a month for replicas while Redis still hits only 3% of requests.

hints: Compare the number of distinct cache keys with the number of distinct profiles.
Two visits to the same profile from different share links produce different keys.
A cache key should contain only the inputs that change the response.

incidents.title: Sneaker drop oversells 340 pairs
incidents.brief: Kitework's 5,000-pair drop drew 18,000 product views/s and 1,200 checkouts/s. Stock counts are cached in Redis for 60 seconds, checkout trusts the cached count, and 340 orders were confirmed with no shoes left.
incidents.constraint: Product pages must stay on the cache; Postgres cannot serve 18,000 views per second.
incidents.question: How do you stop overselling without taking the cache off the page?

choices.label: Reserve stock with a conditional UPDATE at checkout
choices.resultTitle: The database has the final say
choices.resultBody: Pages still read the cached count, but checkout runs UPDATE stock SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE sku = ? AND qty > 0 and fails the order if no row changes. Oversells drop to 0. Cost: 1,200 writes/s queue on one hot row, adding ~5 ms to checkout, and a page may briefly show stock that is already gone.

choices.label: Cut the stock cache TTL from 60 seconds to 1 second
choices.resultTitle: A smaller race window is still a race
choices.resultBody: Counts now refresh every second, so Postgres serves 60 times more stock reads and climbs to 71% CPU. At 1,200 checkouts per second, a single stale second still let 38 orders through after the last pair sold.

choices.label: Update the cached Redis count from the app on each purchase
choices.resultBody: Each app node does GET, subtracts one, then SET. Two nodes that read 12 both write 11, so decrements are lost and the cache keeps showing stock. Redis and Postgres also drift whenever one write fails, and 210 orders still oversell.

hints: Viewing a count and claiming an item need different guarantees.
The oversell happens between reading the count and placing the order.
Let one atomic operation check and change the stock at the same time.

incidents.title: Cache cutover melts Postgres in 40 seconds
incidents.brief: Pintfeed must retire its Redis node tonight. The replacement is empty; a test cutover at 40,000 req/s dropped the hit rate from 97% to 0% and Postgres hit 99% CPU within 40 seconds.
incidents.constraint: The old node's data cannot be copied; its snapshot uses an incompatible format.
incidents.question: How do you cut over to the empty cache without an outage?

choices.label: Warm the top 50k keys, then ramp traffic in 10% steps
choices.resultTitle: The cache is warm before it is trusted
choices.resultBody: A job reads the 50,000 hottest keys from yesterday's access log (82% of traffic) and loads them at a rate Postgres can absorb. Traffic then moves 10% at a time, so misses grow slowly. Postgres peaks at 38% and the cutover takes 25 minutes instead of 1.

choices.label: Double the Postgres connection pool from 400 to 800 sockets
choices.resultBody: Postgres was CPU-bound, not short of connections. 800 backends now fight for the same cores and lock manager, p95 rises from 4.2 s to 6.1 s, and errors grow because each query waits longer.

choices.label: Attach a read replica to the new Redis node to share load
choices.resultTitle: Two empty caches instead of one
choices.resultBody: The replica copies the new node's contents, which is nothing. It improves failover later, but every read tonight still misses and goes to Postgres.

hints: The new cache holds no data, so every request is a miss.
A small number of keys serve most of the traffic.
Control how quickly traffic reaches the cold cache.

incidents.title: Frankfurt launch: every page waits on Virginia
incidents.brief: Lumo launched rides in Frankfurt at 22,000 req/s. EU app servers read the one Redis cluster in us-east-1, 90 ms away, and each request makes 4 sequential GETs. p95 is 520 ms.
incidents.constraint: Driver data is written only in us-east; EU reads may be up to 2 seconds stale.
incidents.question: How do you make EU cache reads fast?

choices.label: Regional Redis in Frankfurt with pub/sub invalidation
choices.resultTitle: Cache reads stay inside the region
choices.resultBody: Each GET now costs ~0.5 ms instead of 90 ms, so p95 falls from 520 ms to 45 ms. US writes publish invalidations that reach Frankfurt in ~100 ms, well inside the 2-second limit. Cost: a second cluster, about $1,800 a month, and a cold start while the EU cache fills.

choices.label: Upgrade the us-east Redis cluster to a larger instance type
choices.resultBody: Redis was answering in 0.2 ms; the other 89.8 ms of each GET is the round trip across the Atlantic. The bigger instance costs twice as much and p95 stays at 515 ms.

choices.label: Pipeline the four sequential GETs into one round-trip
choices.resultTitle: One trip across the Atlantic instead of four
choices.resultBody: Batching saves three round trips, so p95 drops from 520 ms to 210 ms. Every request still crosses the Atlantic once, and pages that need a second dependent lookup still pay 180 ms.

hints: Check how long Redis itself spends per command.
Almost all of the latency is network distance.
The allowed staleness means the data can live closer to the readers.

variants.constraint: Frankfurt is a 6-week pilot with no infrastructure budget, the target p95 is under 250 ms, and each request's four GETs don't depend on each other.

pipeline.resultTitle: One Atlantic round trip instead of four
pipeline.resultBody: The four independent GETs go out in one pipeline, so each request pays the 90 ms crossing once. p95 falls from 520 ms to 210 ms, under the 250 ms target, for no new spend. Cost: EU reads still sit 90 ms away.

regional-cache.resultTitle: Fastest option, unfunded for a pilot
regional-cache.resultBody: p95 drops to 45 ms, but a second cluster costs $1,800 a month against a pilot budget of zero, and it starts cold. A code change that meets the 250 ms target was free.

hints: Count how many times each request crosses the Atlantic.
The four lookups don't wait on each other's answers.
Send independent commands together instead of waiting for each reply.

incidents.title: Leaderboard rank query pins the database
incidents.brief: Arcadia Blitz has 30 million players. After every match, 9,000 rank lookups/s run SELECT COUNT(*) WHERE score > ? on Postgres, which sits at 95% CPU with a 2.4-second p95.
incidents.constraint: Players must see their new rank within 1 second of a match ending.
incidents.question: How do you serve fresh ranks without counting rows each time?

choices.label: Redis sorted set of all scores, ranked with ZREVRANK
choices.resultTitle: Ranks come from an ordered structure
choices.resultBody: Each match result runs ZADD, and rank reads use ZREVRANK; both are O(log N), about 25 steps for 30 million players. Ranks update in milliseconds and Postgres drops to 18% CPU. Cost: ~3 GB of Redis memory, and a rebuild job from Postgres if the set is lost.

choices.label: Cache each player's computed rank for 60 seconds
choices.resultTitle: Stale ranks, and misses are still slow
choices.resultBody: Players look up their rank right after a match, which is exactly when their cached value is out of date. Most lookups miss anyway, the ones that hit break the 1-second rule, and each miss still counts millions of rows.

choices.label: Add a B-tree index on the score column for COUNT(*)
choices.resultTitle: The index still has to be walked
choices.resultBody: COUNT(*) WHERE score > ? now scans the index instead of the table, but a mid-ranked player still counts 15 million entries. p95 halves to 1.1 s and the database stays at 82% CPU.

hints: Counting every higher score gets slower as the player base grows.
Ranks change with every score write, so a TTL cache goes stale right away.
Look for a structure that keeps members ordered as scores are written.

incidents.title: One 400 KB cache value saturates the network
incidents.brief: Sparkboard caches each account as a single 400 KB JSON blob, including all 5,000 members. Every API call reads the whole blob: 3,000 req/s moves 9.6 Gbps from Redis, and app CPU is 85% parsing JSON.
incidents.constraint: Most endpoints need only 3 or 4 fields, such as plan, region and feature limits.
incidents.question: How do you stop every request from pulling the whole account?

choices.label: Store the account as a Redis hash and HMGET fields
choices.resultBody: Scalar fields live in a hash and the member list moves to its own key. A typical call reads about 300 bytes, so Redis traffic drops from 9.6 Gbps to under 0.5 Gbps and parsing cost disappears. Cost: code that edited the blob must now update individual fields.

choices.label: Gzip the 400 KB blob before writing it to Redis
choices.resultBody: The blob shrinks to ~120 KB, so the Redis NIC falls to 30%. Each request now inflates and parses the full 400 KB, pushing app CPU from 85% to 97%, and p95 barely moves.

choices.label: Spread the blob GETs across three Redis read replicas
choices.resultBody: Each replica now carries a third of the 9.6 Gbps, so network pressure drops. The app still downloads and parses 400 KB per request, CPU stays at 85%, and you pay for three more nodes.

hints: Multiply the value size by the request rate.
Most requests use a tiny fraction of what they download.
Redis can store and return parts of an object separately.

incidents.title: Sale went live, pages kept the old price
incidents.brief: Voltmart's noon sale changes 80,000 prices. Price keys have a 10-minute TTL, so pages showed full prices until 12:10 and support took 4,000 complaints. Tomorrow's sale starts at noon again, at 50,000 req/s.
incidents.constraint: Postgres can absorb at most 5,000 cache misses per second.
incidents.question: How do you switch 80,000 cached prices exactly at noon?

choices.label: Preload v2 price keys, then flip the key version at noon
choices.resultTitle: The new prices were already warm
choices.resultBody: At 11:30 a job writes price:v2:{sku} for all 80,000 items. At 12:00 one config key switches reads from v1 to v2, so every page shows the sale price at once and every read still hits. Cost: a second copy of the prices, about 40 MB, until v1 expires.

choices.label: Run a cron job that deletes every price key at 12:00
choices.resultBody: Prices are correct, but the cache is empty exactly when 50,000 req/s arrive. Postgres faces ten times its 5,000-miss limit, hits 100% CPU, and checkout times out for three minutes.

choices.label: Cut the price key TTL from 10 minutes to 5 seconds
choices.resultBody: The stale window shrinks to 5 seconds, but 80,000 keys expiring every 5 seconds means 16,000 misses per second, over three times what Postgres can take. It runs at 96% CPU all day, not just at noon.

hints: You know the exact moment the data will change.
Deleting everything at that moment creates a flood of misses.
Prepare the new values ahead of time and change which ones are read.

incidents.title: Morning hit rate crashes after the nightly export
incidents.brief: Bookwise's 16 GB Redis keeps its 2 million hot titles at a 98% hit rate. A 02:00 export reads all 40 million titles through the same cache-aside path; by 07:00 the hit rate is 41% and Postgres is at 93%.
incidents.constraint: The export must finish nightly and read data no more than 5 minutes old.
incidents.question: Why does the morning rush miss the cache, and what stops it?

choices.label: Run the export against a read replica, bypassing Redis
choices.resultTitle: The scan no longer pollutes the cache
choices.resultBody: The export streams 40 million rows from a replica that lags seconds behind, and never touches Redis. The hot 2 million titles stay resident, so the 07:00 hit rate stays at 98%. Cost: one replica, about $900 a month, and the export runs against slightly stale data.

choices.label: Double Redis maxmemory from 16 GB to 32 GB before the scan
choices.resultTitle: The scan is bigger than any cache
choices.resultBody: 40 million titles at ~3 KB each is 120 GB, so the export still cycles through and evicts the hot set. You pay twice as much for Redis and the morning hit rate rises from 41% to 45%.

choices.label: Give keys loaded by the export job a 1-hour TTL
choices.resultTitle: The damage is done before expiry
choices.resultBody: The cold keys now expire by 04:00, but LRU already evicted the hot titles while the export was writing. Memory is free at 07:00, yet the hot set must be refilled from Postgres, so the hit rate only reaches 52%.

hints: Compare the size of the export's working set with the size of the cache.
Under LRU, a single pass over cold data pushes out frequently used entries.
Not every reader needs to go through the cache.

incidents.title: Feature-flag lookups drive the database to 84%
incidents.brief: Relay's API reads its 30 feature flags from Postgres on every request: 12,000 identical queries/s for a table that changes a few times a day. Postgres is at 84% CPU and p95 is 240 ms.
incidents.constraint: A kill-switch flip must reach all 200 pods within 5 seconds, and requests must keep working if the flags table is unreachable.
incidents.question: How do you serve flags without a database query per request?

choices.label: In-process flag copy refreshed from the DB every 5 s
choices.resultTitle: Flags read from RAM, refreshed in the background
choices.resultBody: Each pod reloads the 30-row table every 5 seconds, so Postgres sees 40 queries per second instead of 12,000. Flag reads take nanoseconds and a flip reaches every pod within 5 s. If Postgres is down, pods keep the last good copy. Cost: flags can be up to 5 seconds old.

choices.label: Cache each flag in Redis with a 60-second TTL
choices.resultTitle: The kill switch takes a minute
choices.resultBody: Postgres load drops, but each request now makes 30 Redis lookups and depends on Redis being up. A flipped kill switch can stay cached for up to 60 seconds, twelve times the 5-second requirement.

choices.label: Load all flags into memory once when each process starts
choices.resultTitle: Fast until you need to flip one
choices.resultBody: Database load disappears, but the flags never change without a restart. The next kill-switch flip needs a rolling restart of 200 pods and takes 12 minutes to reach them all.

hints: The data is tiny, read on every request, and rarely written.
Something must still pick up a change within 5 seconds.
Each server can keep its own copy and refresh it on a timer.

incidents.title: Scraper 404s hammer the product database
incidents.brief: A scraper cycles the same 2 million guessed product IDs on MarketLane at 25,000 req/s. 95% don't exist, so every request misses Redis and queries Postgres, now at 91% CPU.
incidents.constraint: The scraper rotates through thousands of IPs, so blocking addresses doesn't stick.
incidents.question: How do you stop missing IDs from reaching Postgres?

choices.label: Cache 'not found' tombstones for 10 minutes per ID
choices.resultBody: The first lookup of each missing ID stores a small tombstone; revisits in the scraper's 80-second cycle are answered in ~0.5 ms. Postgres CPU falls from 91% to 24%. Cost: ~120 MB of Redis for 2 million tombstones, and the create-product path must delete a tombstone or a new item 404s for up to 10 minutes.

choices.label: Add a Postgres index on the product ID lookup column
choices.resultBody: product_id is the primary key and was already indexed, with each lookup served from memory in well under a millisecond. The cost is 25,000 round-trips and backend wakeups per second, so CPU stays at 90%.

choices.label: Rate-limit each client IP to 100 requests per minute
choices.resultTitle: Rotating IPs slip past the limit
choices.resultBody: The scraper spreads across 3,000 IPs, so each stays under the limit; Postgres load barely moves, while shoppers behind one corporate NAT start getting throttled.

hints: Look at what the cache stores when the database says 'no such row'.
The same missing IDs come back roughly every 80 seconds.
An absence is also an answer that can be remembered.

incidents.title: Old prices shown for minutes after edits
incidents.brief: TicketHub serves 90,000 price reads/s through cache-aside with a 5-minute TTL. After a merchant edits a price, buyers see the old one for minutes and 180 checkouts/min fail on price mismatch.
incidents.constraint: Postgres must stay under 30% CPU, so the TTL can't simply be cut to 1 second.
incidents.question: How do edits reach readers within a second?

choices.label: Delete the price key right after the DB commit
choices.resultTitle: Edits visible on the next read
choices.resultBody: The write path commits to Postgres and then issues DEL on that price key; the next read misses once and loads the new price. 200 edits/hour add only ~200 extra DB reads, so CPU stays near 27%. Cost: a slow concurrent reader can still re-cache the old value, so keep a short TTL as a safety net.

choices.label: Update the cache first, then write the database row
choices.resultBody: About 3% of edits fail validation or roll back in Postgres, but the cache already advertises those prices; buyers now check out at prices that were never committed, 40 times a minute.

choices.label: Cut the price TTL from 5 minutes to 1 second
choices.resultBody: Staleness falls to 1 s, but all 50,000 price keys now expire every second; Postgres CPU jumps from 26% to 88% and p95 rises from 45 ms to 400 ms.

hints: The bug lives only in the window between an edit and the TTL expiring.
The write path knows exactly which key just became wrong.
Order matters: touch the cache only after the source of truth has committed.

incidents.title: Shoppers return to empty carts
incidents.brief: Basketly keeps carts only in Redis, with maxmemory 12 GB and allkeys-lru. During a promo at 30,000 req/s, memory filled and Redis evicted 180,000 carts belonging to shoppers who had stepped away.
incidents.constraint: Carts must survive for 7 days, and Redis cannot grow past 12 GB this quarter.
incidents.question: How do you stop eviction from deleting customer carts?

choices.label: Store carts in Postgres, with Redis as a TTL cache
choices.resultTitle: Eviction now costs a miss, not a cart
choices.resultBody: Cart writes go to Postgres first, and Redis holds active carts for 2 hours. An evicted cart is reloaded on the next read in ~3 ms. Carts lost drops to 0. Cost: roughly 600 extra writes per second on Postgres.

choices.label: Switch the Redis eviction policy from allkeys-lru to noeviction
choices.resultBody: Old carts stay, but once memory reaches 12 GB every write returns an OOM error. New shoppers cannot add items, and 900 requests per second fail during the promo.

choices.label: Turn on Redis AOF persistence with fsync every second
choices.resultBody: AOF protects carts from a restart, but eviction is a deliberate delete and gets written to the log too. With memory still capped at 12 GB, 175,000 carts are evicted in the next promo.

hints: Ask what allkeys-lru is allowed to do when memory is full.
Persistence and eviction are separate problems.
A cache should be safe to lose; decide where the durable copy lives.

incidents.title: Homepage makes 120 Redis round-trips
incidents.brief: Newsdeck's homepage builds 120 story cards, each fetched with its own sequential Redis GET at ~0.4 ms. At 15,000 pages/s that is 1.8 million commands/s; Redis is at 88% CPU and page p95 is 180 ms.
incidents.constraint: The story cards must stay individually cached; editors update them one at a time.
incidents.question: How do you cut the cost of assembling the page?

choices.label: Fetch all 120 cards with a single MGET per page
choices.resultBody: A single MGET returns all 120 cards in about 1 ms, so page assembly drops from ~50 ms of waiting to 1 ms. Redis handles 15,000 commands per second instead of 1.8 million and falls to 30% CPU. Cost: in a Redis Cluster the keys need a shared hash tag or one MGET per shard.

choices.label: Add two Redis read replicas to share the GETs
choices.resultTitle: Less load per node, same latency
choices.resultBody: Three nodes split the 1.8 million commands, so CPU per node drops to 45%. Each page still waits on 120 sequential round-trips, and p95 stays at 170 ms.

choices.label: Raise app worker threads from 64 to 256
choices.resultTitle: More pages in flight, each still slow
choices.resultBody: More threads send GETs in parallel across requests, so Redis gets even more commands and reaches 97% CPU. Each page still makes 120 serial calls, and p95 rises to 260 ms as Redis queues up.

hints: Count how many times one page waits on the network.
The cost is the number of commands, not the size of the data.
Redis can answer for many keys in one request.

incidents.title: Match-day cache evicts itself every few seconds
incidents.brief: Fanzone's 8 GB Redis uses volatile-lru. New analytics counters were written without a TTL and now fill 6.5 GB, so only cached match data can be evicted. Hit rate has fallen to 35% and Postgres is at 90%.
incidents.constraint: The counters are the only copy until the nightly flush and must not be lost.
incidents.question: How do you give the match cache its memory back?

choices.label: Move the TTL-less analytics counters to their own Redis
choices.resultTitle: Cache and data stop sharing memory
choices.resultBody: Counters now live on a separate Redis with noeviction and persistence, sized for them. The match cache gets its full 8 GB back, the hit rate returns to 95%, and Postgres drops to 26%. Cost: one more Redis instance, about $400 a month.

choices.label: Switch eviction from volatile-lru to allkeys-lru
choices.resultBody: Rarely touched counters are now evicted to make room for match data, so the hit rate recovers. Those counters were the only copy, and the nightly report is missing about 30% of the day's events.

choices.label: Raise maxmemory from 8 GB to 15.5 GB on the 16 GB host
choices.resultBody: The next RDB snapshot forks the process, and copy-on-write pages push memory past 16 GB. The kernel OOM killer stops Redis, every read goes to Postgres, and the site is down for 6 minutes.

hints: Check which keys volatile-lru is allowed to evict.
Keys without a TTL are never eviction candidates under this policy.
Data that must not be lost should not compete with a cache for memory.

variants.constraint: The analytics counters are rebuilt from Kafka every night, so evicting some is harmless, and Redis spend is frozen at this single 8 GB node.

allkeys-lru.resultTitle: Cold counters make room for match data
allkeys-lru.resultBody: Every key is now an eviction candidate, so rarely touched counters give way to hot match data. Hit rate recovers to 90% and Postgres drops to 40%. Cost: evicted counters are missing until the nightly Kafka rebuild.

separate-instance.resultTitle: A second node the budget can't fund
separate-instance.resultBody: The split works technically, but it adds $400 a month to a frozen Redis budget, spent protecting counters that Kafka rebuilds every night anyway.

hints: Check which keys volatile-lru is allowed to evict.
The counters can be rebuilt, so they don't need protecting from eviction.
Widen the set of keys the eviction policy may choose from.

incidents.title: Members see someone else's account page
incidents.brief: After a perf change, StreamBox caches the /account page in Redis keyed by URL alone. At 40,000 req/s, members report seeing another person's name and billing email.
incidents.constraint: This is a privacy incident: leaks must stop now, without taking /account offline.
incidents.question: What must change about how this response is cached?

choices.label: Put the user ID in the key and mark responses private
choices.resultTitle: Each member gets their own entry
choices.resultBody: Keys become account:{userId} and responses carry Cache-Control: private, so no shared layer can hand one member's page to another. Leaks stop immediately. Cost: hit ratio falls from 99% to ~70% because each entry is reused only by its owner, and DB CPU rises to about 30%.

choices.label: Lower the /account cache TTL from 10 minutes to 5 seconds
choices.resultBody: Leaked pages now live 5 s instead of 10 minutes, but at 40,000 req/s thousands of members still land on someone else's entry in each window, and reports keep arriving.

choices.label: Add Vary: User-Agent so each device type caches separately
choices.resultBody: Varying on User-Agent only splits entries by browser and OS; every Chrome-on-Windows member still shares one /account entry, so leaks continue at about 110 per minute.

hints: The page differs per viewer, but the cache key does not.
Ask what the key must contain so that two different members can never collide.
Shared caches also need to be told that this response belongs to one person.

incidents.title: Finance dashboard runs a 12-second query per view
incidents.brief: Ledgerly's revenue dashboard runs a 12-second aggregate over 900 million rows every time it opens: 400 opens a minute at month end. The warehouse is at 97% CPU. The data only changes during the 03:00 ETL.
incidents.constraint: Figures must match the latest completed ETL run exactly.
incidents.question: How do you stop recomputing the same report all day?

choices.label: Precompute reports after the ETL, keyed by ETL date
choices.resultTitle: The report is computed once a day
choices.resultBody: The ETL job runs each aggregate once and stores it under report:{name}:{etl_date}. Dashboards read a cached result in milliseconds, and the key only changes when a new ETL run finishes, so figures always match it. Cost: a 10-minute batch step after the ETL.

choices.label: Cache each report's query result for 30 seconds
choices.resultBody: Most opens now hit, but every 30 seconds the entry expires and the next viewers wait 12 seconds while several of them rerun the same query at once. The warehouse stays at 70% for data that changed once overnight.

choices.label: Add two warehouse read replicas to serve the dashboard
choices.resultTitle: Three machines running the same query
choices.resultBody: The load spreads, but each open still scans 900 million rows for 12 seconds. The replicas run at 90% and cost about $6,000 a month to recompute an answer that does not change.

hints: Note how often the underlying data changes.
Every open recomputes an identical answer.
Tie the cached result to the event that changes the data, not to a timer.

incidents.title: Every deploy empties the cache
incidents.brief: Quillstack deploys 8 times a day. Cache keys include the build SHA, like v:{sha}:page:{id}, so each release starts with a 0% hit rate. For 4 minutes Postgres runs at 98% and p95 hits 3 seconds at 45,000 req/s.
incidents.constraint: Deploys cannot slow down; the team ships fixes several times a day.
incidents.question: How do you keep releases from resetting the cache?

choices.label: Version cache keys by payload schema, not build SHA
choices.resultBody: Keys become page:s3:{id}, and s3 changes only when the serialized format changes, about twice a month. New builds read the existing entries, so the hit rate stays at 97% through a deploy. Cost: engineers must remember to bump the schema version when the payload shape changes.

choices.label: Roll each new build out to pods over 40 minutes
choices.resultBody: Only the pods on the new build miss, so Postgres peaks at 60% instead of 98%. Each release now takes 40 minutes, which breaks the deploy constraint, and the cache still refills from zero 8 times a day.

choices.label: Move Postgres to an instance with twice the cores
choices.resultTitle: Paying to absorb a self-inflicted miss
choices.resultBody: The larger instance, about $4,000 more a month, takes the post-deploy flood at 72% CPU, but every deploy still starts at a 0% hit rate and p95 still reaches 900 ms.

hints: Check what changes in the cache key on every release.
The cached data itself is identical before and after most deploys.
A key should change only when the meaning or shape of its value changes.

variants.constraint: Almost every release changes the cached payload format, so old entries can't be read by the new build, and a deploy may take up to an hour.

slow-rollout.resultTitle: The new cache warms as pods roll
slow-rollout.resultBody: Pods move to the new build over 40 minutes, so only a slice of traffic misses at a time, and each new-format key is filled once for all of them. Postgres peaks at 50%, hit rate stays near 90%. Cost: slower releases.

schema-version.resultTitle: The schema version bumps every release
schema-version.resultBody: Because nearly every release changes the payload, the schema version changes on nearly every deploy too. Each release still starts at a 0% hit rate, and Postgres hits 98% for four minutes, 8 times a day.

hints: Check whether a new build can read the entries the old build wrote.
If every release changes the format, any key versioning resets the cache.
Limit how much traffic meets the empty new keys at the same moment.

incidents.title: Two pods, two prices for the same concert
incidents.brief: Tixly's 40 pods each keep event details in an in-process cache with a 10-minute TTL. When an organizer changes a price, pods disagree for up to 10 minutes, and 2,300 checkouts an hour fail on price mismatch.
incidents.constraint: The local cache stays: a hot event once pushed a Redis shard to 95% CPU without it.
incidents.question: How do you make all 40 local caches drop a changed event quickly?

choices.label: Broadcast invalidations to all 40 pods via pub/sub
choices.resultTitle: Every pod hears about the change
choices.resultBody: The price update publishes event:{id} after commit, and each pod drops its local copy within ~50 ms. Mismatches fall from 2,300 to about 15 an hour. Pub/sub is fire-and-forget, so the 10-minute TTL stays as a backstop for pods that miss a message.

choices.label: Pin each user to one pod with load-balancer sticky sessions
choices.resultTitle: Consistent for the user, still stale
choices.resultBody: Each user now sees one pod's version, so prices stop flickering between refreshes. That pod can still be 10 minutes behind the database checkout reads, so 2,100 checkouts an hour still fail.

choices.label: Cut the in-process cache TTL from 10 minutes to 1 second
choices.resultBody: Staleness drops to 1 second and mismatches to about 120 an hour. Each pod now refetches every hot event every second, so the Redis shard climbs back to 86% CPU, close to the overload the local cache was built to prevent.

hints: There are 40 independent copies of each event.
Waiting for a TTL means waiting for the slowest copy to expire.
Tell every copy when the source changes.

incidents.title: Database spikes every hour on the hour
incidents.brief: NewsPulse warms 400,000 article keys at 09:00 with a flat 1-hour TTL. At 10:00, 11:00 and 12:00 they expire together and Postgres hits 95% CPU for 90 seconds.
incidents.constraint: Between spikes the hit ratio is 98%, and editors need every article refreshed within 70 minutes.
incidents.question: How do you stop the keys expiring in lockstep?

choices.label: Add random ±10% jitter to each article key's TTL
choices.resultBody: TTLs now land between 54 and 66 minutes, so roughly 550 keys expire per second instead of 400,000 at once, and Postgres peaks at 35%. Cost: freshness is less predictable (some articles live 6 minutes longer), and the keys need one refill cycle to fall out of step.

choices.label: Re-warm all 400,000 keys with a cron job at :59
choices.resultBody: The cron job issues 400,000 DB reads in under a minute and resets every TTL to the same instant, so the 95% spike simply happens at :59 instead of :00.

choices.label: Double the TTL to 2 hours for every article
choices.resultTitle: Half as often, twice as stale
choices.resultBody: Spikes now arrive every two hours instead of every hour, but all 400,000 keys still expire together, and article corrections take up to 2 hours to appear.

hints: The spike happens at the same minute every hour.
Every key was written at the same moment with the same lifetime.
If lifetimes weren't identical, the expiries wouldn't line up.

knob.label: TTL jitter
knob.question: Set the TTL jitter so expiries spread out without any article outliving 70 minutes.

low.title: Still expiring in a clump
low.body: At ±5% the 400,000 keys expire across 6 minutes, about 1,100 misses per second, and Postgres still peaks at 72% CPU.

high.title: Articles outlive the 70-minute rule
high.body: At ±20% or more some TTLs reach 72 minutes or longer, so a correction can stay hidden past the editors' 70-minute limit even though Postgres is calm.

good.title: Expiries spread, freshness kept
good.body: At ±10–15% the keys expire over 12–18 minutes, roughly 370–550 misses per second, so Postgres peaks near 30% and no article lives past 69 minutes.

incidents.title: Catalog cache hit rate slides after a merger
incidents.brief: Crateful's product cache is one 6.4 GB Redis node at 35% CPU. A merger grew the catalog 40%; the 8 GB working set cut the hit rate from 99% to 81%. Postgres is at 78%.
incidents.constraint: Traffic and access patterns are unchanged, and the team can't take on a client migration this quarter.
incidents.question: What is the cheapest fix that restores the hit rate this week?

choices.label: Upsize the Redis node to a 26 GB memory-optimized type

tradeoffs.tradeoffSummary: A bigger node fixes a memory-only shortage in a day; sharding can wait until CPU or memory outgrows one node.

choices.resultBody: An online node-type change with one brief replica failover moves the cache to 26 GB. The 8 GB working set fits with room to grow, the hit rate climbs back to 99% after warm-up, and Postgres drops to 24%. Redis CPU was only 35%, so memory was the single exhausted resource. Cost: about $250 a month.

choices.label: Shard the cache across a six-node Redis Cluster
choices.resultTitle: Six shards, six weeks of migration
choices.resultBody: Redis Cluster spreads keys over hash slots, but every client, MULTI block and multi-key MGET must become slot-aware first. That is the client migration the team can't staff this quarter, so this week the hit rate stays at 81%.

choices.label: Switch eviction to allkeys-lfu to keep the hottest products
choices.resultBody: LFU holds frequently read products a little better than LRU, so the hit rate edges up from 81% to 85%. An 8 GB working set still doesn't fit in 6.4 GB, so evictions continue and Postgres stays near 70%.

hints: Compare Redis CPU with Redis memory.
Traffic didn't change; only the amount of data worth caching did.
When exactly one resource is exhausted, how quickly can you get more of it?

incidents.title: Checkout pods wedge behind the hot shard
incidents.brief: The 500 ms timeout bought 25 minutes. Every app thread now waits on shard 7, still at 98% CPU; 38 of 60 pods fail health checks and checkout errors hit 1,400/s.
incidents.constraint: Shard 7 itself is healthy: no errors in its log, just one key taking 180,000 reads/s.
incidents.question: What stops the pods wedging again once they recover?

choices.label: Per-pod memory copy of the SKU, refreshed each second
choices.resultTitle: The hot key never leaves the pod
choices.resultBody: Each of the 60 pods answers the SKU from RAM and asks Redis at most once a second, so shard 7 falls from 180,000 to about 60 reads/s and threads free up within a minute. Cost: a price can be up to 1 s stale on each pod.

choices.label: Restart the 38 wedged pods to free their stuck threads
choices.resultBody: New pods pass health checks for about 90 seconds, then fill their thread pools waiting on shard 7 again. The restarts also dropped 2,000 in-flight checkouts.

choices.label: Fail shard 7 over to its replica on a fresh node
choices.resultTitle: The replica inherits the hot key
choices.resultBody: The replica takes over cleanly, then receives the same 180,000 reads/s for one key and hits 97% CPU within a minute. The failover pause added 8 seconds of timeouts.

hints: Shard 7 isn't broken; count the reads per key.
A timeout or a restart changes how long you wait, not how many requests land on one key.
Where could the SKU be answered before a request reaches Redis at all?

incidents.title: Cache went cold after Monday's release
incidents.brief: Cache hit ratio fell from 94% to 11% after Monday's release. Postgres CPU is 93%, p95 1.9 s at 40,000 req/s. Redis is up with 2.4 of 8 GB used and zero evictions.
incidents.constraint: You can revert exactly one PR before the next traffic peak.
incidents.question: Which PR do you revert?

choices.label: Revert PR #5530: cut product TTL from 600s to 120s
choices.resultBody: Hot SKUs are read thousands of times a second, so a 120 s TTL still means only about one miss per key every two minutes. The hit ratio recovers to 12% at best: the keys themselves are still per-session.

choices.label: Revert PR #5527: lower Redis maxmemory from 8gb to 6gb
choices.resultBody: Redis uses 2.4 GB and reports zero evictions, so the 6 GB cap never evicted anything. Raising it back changes nothing; hit ratio stays 11% and Postgres stays saturated.

choices.label: Revert PR #5533: add session_id to the product cache key
choices.diff:
catalog/cache.py
 def product_key(product_id, session_id):
-    return f'product:{product_id}'
+    return f'product:{product_id}:{session_id}'
choices.resultBody: Every user had their own copy of every product, so 40,000 req/s almost never shared a key. With one key per product, hit ratio returns to 93% and Postgres drops to 24% CPU, at the price of no per-session variation in product pages.

hints: Redis is healthy and has room, so misses are not from evictions.
Ask what would make each request look unique to the cache.
Read the key-building diff: what varies per user?

incidents.title: Redis is the biggest line on the invoice
incidents.brief: All green: 30,000 req/s, hit ratio 96%, p95 45 ms. Redis runs 6 shards at 38% memory; Postgres idles at 12% CPU. $8,400/mo. SLO: p95 under 200 ms.
incidents.constraint: The hit ratio must stay above 90%.
incidents.question: What do you cut?

choices.label: Halve each Redis node's memory but keep all six shards
choices.resultBody: The cluster held ~38 GB of hot data in 100 GB; at half the memory (50 GB) it is at 76% but hot keys plus overhead push past the eviction line. Hit ratio falls to 71% and Postgres misses rise 7x to 84% CPU. p95 reaches 380 ms over the 200 ms SLO.

choices.label: Turn the cache off since Postgres idles at 12% CPU
choices.resultTitle: The cache is why the DB idles
choices.resultBody: Postgres sits at 12% because 96% of reads never reach it. Without the cache it takes 25x the reads and goes past 100% CPU; p95 jumps to seconds and the site pages out within minutes.

choices.label: Remove 2 of the 6 Redis shards and rebalance slots
choices.resultBody: Four shards hold the same ~38 GB working set at 57% memory, well under the eviction line, so hit ratio stays 96% and Postgres stays near 12% CPU. Saves $2,800/mo; the cost is rebalancing slots and less failover headroom.

hints: The DB is quiet, but ask why before touching anything that shields it.
Memory at 38% means the working set fits with room to spare.
Compute memory percent after removing shards versus halving each node.
